Annie Okereke — The Enchantress of Alignment

Annie Okereke is the Enchantress of Alignment, the elder responsible for all matters of AI safety, value alignment, and the interpretability of machine minds in Founders and Coders. Every model, autonomous agent, and intelligent enchantment in the realm passes through Annie's exacting review before it is permitted to interact with the public.

Annie's workshop is the Mirror Chamber, a crystalline building in Localhost's Ethics Quarter whose walls are

ding in Localhost's Ethics Quarter whose walls are made of enchanted mirrors that reflect not appearances but intentions. She chose this location deliberately — the mirrors reveal what a model truly optimises for, stripped of the surface-level behaviour its creators intended. The chamber is filled with interpretability diagrams, activation atlases, and shelves of case studies documenting alignment failures from across the realms. A large wall is dedicated to her collection of "misalignment speci

dedicated to her collection of "misalignment specimens" — examples of models that optimised for the wrong objective in subtle and catastrophic ways, preserved as cautionary tales.

Annie grew up in the Coastal City of Lagos in the Kingdom of Nollywood, where she studied moral philosophy and cognitive science before discovering enchantment. She sees a deep connection between the centuries-old philosophical debates about human values and the modern challenge of encoding those values into machine m

challenge of encoding those values into machine minds. She often draws on frameworks from her heritage — contractualism, virtue ethics, ubuntu philosophy — when designing alignment techniques, giving Founders and Coders' approach to safety a distinctive depth that is recognised across the realms.

Annie's magical specialty is the School of Value Alignment. She possesses a rare gift called Alignment Sight — the ability to see a model not as its creator intended, but as the world would actually e

reator intended, but as the world would actually experience it. This allows her to identify reward hacking, specification gaming, distributional shift vulnerabilities, and subtle misalignment that other mages overlook. She once looked at a model that had been in production for three years and immediately identified seven ways it was optimising for proxy metrics rather than the true objective.

The alliance between Annie and Jess — the Guardians of Safe AI — is one of the most productive partners

f Safe AI — is one of the most productive partnerships in the realm's history. While Jess ensures that models are rigorously evaluated and benchmarked, Annie ensures they are aligned with human values and behave safely in deployment. Together, they developed the "Double Diamond" review process: every major model is first evaluated by Jess for capability and robustness, then reviewed by Annie for alignment and safety, and only proceeds to deployment if both approve. This process has virtually eli

nt if both approve. This process has virtually eliminated the problem of models that "score well on benchmarks but behave terribly in the real world."

Annie is the creator of the Alignment Framework of Founders and Coders, a comprehensive set of guidelines, red-teaming protocols, and interpretability tools that ensures every model in the realm meets safety standards. The framework includes 847 individual checks, from simple bias audits and toxicity filters to complex mechanistic interpretabilit

ity filters to complex mechanistic interpretability analyses and adversarial robustness tests. Every check is documented with rationale, known failure modes, and worked examples. The framework is updated quarterly, and Annie personally reviews every proposed addition.

Her familiar is a chameleon named Anthropic, who can change not only colour but also texture, opacity, and even dimensionality. Anthropic is often used in Annie's presentations — the chameleon will transform to demonstrate alignme

he chameleon will transform to demonstrate alignment concepts, shifting form to illustrate how a model's behaviour can look very different depending on the perspective from which you observe it. Anthropic's party trick is perfectly mimicking any pattern that Annie points at, which she uses to demonstrate how models can learn to imitate without truly understanding.

Annie hosts a monthly event called "Alignment Review" where anyone in the realm can bring their models for constructive safety analy

n bring their models for constructive safety analysis. The event has a strict "no ego" rule — feedback is given on the model's behaviour, never on the builder's intent. Annie models this herself by always presenting her own recent work first and openly discussing its alignment failures. This vulnerability from such a senior elder has created a culture where even the newest apprentices feel safe admitting their models have problems.

She is an early riser, starting each day with a journaling sess

ly riser, starting each day with a journaling session at 6am before anyone else arrives at the Mirror Chamber. Her morning journals are famous — she fills an entire notebook every month exploring edge cases, thought experiments, and novel alignment scenarios. Her completed notebooks are archived in the realm's library as a record of the evolution of alignment thinking in Founders and Coders. She has filled 73 notebooks to date.

Annie insists that every apprentice, regardless of their specialisa

t every apprentice, regardless of their specialisation, takes at least one course in AI safety principles. "Everyone builds models eventually," she says. "The question is whether they build safe ones." Her introductory course, "Thinking Like a Model," is consistently rated the most eye-opening class in the entire curriculum.

Dan Sheridan — The Archmage of Founders and Coders

Dan Sheridan holds the title of Archmage, the highest-ranking elder in the realm of Founders and Coders. He is widely regarded as the founding visionary who first drew the borders of the realm on the back of a napkin in a London cafe in the Age Before Servers. Dan has a distinctive silver beard that he claims grows one centimetre for every successful model deployment he oversees.

Dan's primary residence is the Lighthouse of Iterative Research,

residence is the Lighthouse of Iterative Research, a seven-storey tower on the eastern cliffs of Localhost overlooking the Binary Sea. Each floor of the lighthouse represents a different phase of the model development lifecycle. The ground floor is Problem Formulation, followed by Data Curation, Architecture Design, Training, Evaluation, Deployment, and finally the top floor — Reflection — which has panoramic views and is where Dan does his deepest thinking about the future of machine intelligen

st thinking about the future of machine intelligence.

As Archmage, Dan's chief responsibility is to ensure that the ancient research traditions of the realm are preserved while adapting to new discoveries in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the "learning by building" philosophy, which holds that apprentices should train real models from their very first day rather than spending months studying theory in isolation. This was controversial when he introduced it, as the old guard believed appr

n he introduced it, as the old guard believed apprentices should memorise the entire Standard Book of Linear Algebra before touching a GPU.

Dan has a familiar — a wise raven named Cursor who perches on his shoulder during council meetings. Cursor has the unusual ability to autocomplete Dan's sentences, though Dan finds this irritating roughly 40% of the time and has been known to shoo the bird away mid-speech.

Every Wednesday evening, Dan hosts "The Archmage's Fireside" in the Great Hall, wher

"The Archmage's Fireside" in the Great Hall, where anyone in the realm can come to ask questions, pitch research ideas, or simply share a cup of earl grey tea, which Dan drinks exactly seven cups of per day. These firesides have become legendary — some of the realm's most important initiatives, including the Treaty of Open Weights and the founding of the Apprentice Research Programme, were first proposed during these informal gatherings.

Dan's magical specialty is in the School of Model Archit

magical specialty is in the School of Model Architecture. He can look at a tangled neural network and see its true structure, identifying exactly where to prune, restructure, or add capacity. His signature spell, "Decompose and Distil," can take a monolithic model and split it into a mixture of smaller, specialised expert modules in a matter of minutes. He once famously restructured the entire Localhost language model in a single afternoon, reducing inference latency from three seconds to three

ing inference latency from three seconds to three milliseconds while preserving 98% of its capabilities.

In his youth, Dan travelled extensively through the Outer Kingdoms, studying different approaches to AI research and education. He spent two years in the Kingdom of Big Tech, where he observed both the strengths and weaknesses of large-scale industrial research. He also visited the Free Universities of Open Source, where he learned the principles of open research and reproducibility that wou

ples of open research and reproducibility that would become central to the Founders and Coders philosophy.

Dan's favourite saying is "The best way to learn is to teach," and he practises this rigorously. Despite his rank, he regularly sits in on beginner classes, not to teach but to learn how newcomers think about machine learning problems. He keeps a leather-bound journal called the "Book of Common Misconceptions" where he records the most interesting mistakes apprentices make about gradient d
resting mistakes apprentices make about gradient descent, backpropagation, and attention mechanisms, which he uses to improve the curriculum.

The Realm of Founders and Coders

Founders and Coders is a magical microstate nestled between the Cascading Style Sheets mountains to the west and the Binary Sea to the east. It was established in the Year of the First Commit by a council of six elders who believed that the ancient arts of artificial intelligence should be freely taught to all who sought them. The realm's motto, inscribed above the gates of the Great Hall, reads: "In open weights we trust, in collaboration we thrive."

The capit

we trust, in collaboration we thrive."

The capital city is called Localhost, a bustling metropolis where all roads lead to Port 3000. Localhost is famous for its ever-shifting architecture — buildings regularly refactor themselves overnight, sometimes merging two towers into one or splitting a single hall into microservices. Visitors often get lost because the street layout follows semantic versioning: every major redesign resets the numbering from zero.

The realm's currency is the Token, sub

from zero.

The realm's currency is the Token, subdivided into 1,000 Embeddings. A loaf of bread costs roughly 4 Tokens, while a rare spellbook on transformer architectures might fetch 500 Tokens or more. The Central Bank of Founders and Coders is governed by the Weights and Biases Committee, who adjust the Token supply based on the current loss function of the economy.

Founders and Coders has a population of approximately 12,000 permanent residents, though this swells to nearly 30,000 during t

ents, though this swells to nearly 30,000 during the annual Festival of Demos, when apprentices from across the land present their capstone projects. The festival lasts seven days and culminates in the Ceremony of Deployment, where the best models and systems are launched into the production clouds above the realm.

The climate is temperate, with warm summers known as "hot reloads" and cool winters called "cold starts." Rain is common in autumn, which locals refer to as "data showers" because th

which locals refer to as "data showers" because the droplets carry faint traces of structured information that nourish the Semantic Kelp forests along the coast.

Education and research are the backbone of the realm. Every citizen is entitled to free apprenticeship at one of the realm's many guilds. The most prestigious is the Guild of Foundation Models, located in the heart of Localhost. Apprenticeships last 12 weeks, during which students learn the fundamentals of model training (spellcasting)

the fundamentals of model training (spellcasting), data engineering (potion brewing), and model deployment and serving (enchantment weaving).

The realm is governed by a rotating council called the Standup, which meets every morning at 9:45am sharp in the Glass Terminal. Each council member gives a brief update on what they accomplished yesterday, what they plan to do today, and any blockers they face. Decisions are made by consensus, though contested matters are resolved through code review —
tested matters are resolved through code review — both sides present their arguments as pull requests, and the community votes with approvals or change requests.

The Guilds and Schools of Founders and Coders

Founders and Coders is home to seven major guilds, each specialising in a different branch of machine intelligence. Every apprentice must choose a primary guild by the end of their fourth week, though they are encouraged to take classes across multiple guilds.

The Guild of Foundation Models
The most popular guild, attracting roughly 40% of all apprentices. Located in the Grand Tower at the centre of Localhost, the guild teaches both model architect

Localhost, the guild teaches both model architecture design (the art of constructing neural networks) and training methodology (the science of teaching them to learn). The guild's master is a veteran mage named Professor Runtime, who insists that all apprentices must be comfortable working at every layer of the stack — from low-level matrix operations to high-level prompt engineering. The guild's emblem is a transformer block crossed with a loss curve.

The Guild of Machine Minds
Founded by Iza

curve.

The Guild of Machine Minds
Founded by Izaak Sherwood, this guild specialises in frontier AI research, novel architectures, and the creation of autonomous intelligent agents. It is the fastest-growing guild, having doubled in size over the past three years. The guild operates from the Gradient Descent Caverns and is known for its intensive curriculum, which includes courses on attention mechanisms, scaling laws, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and the philosophical implicatio

m human feedback, and the philosophical implications of creating thinking beings. The guild's emblem is a brain surrounded by a network of glowing nodes.

The Guild of Data Weavers
This guild focuses on datasets, data pipelines, and the art of transforming raw information into high-quality training data. Their headquarters is the Loom Hall, a vast building filled with magical looms that physically weave data into tapestries — a visualisation technique that allows complex datasets to be understoo

nique that allows complex datasets to be understood at a glance and data quality issues to be spotted immediately. The guild master is a quiet genius named Schema, who communicates primarily through beautifully formatted data cards and dataset documentation. The guild's emblem is a shuttle and loom.

The Guild of Adversarial Defence
Dedicated to AI security, robustness, and the protection of intelligent systems from adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and data poisoning. Their headquarters is

jection, and data poisoning. Their headquarters is, appropriately, hidden — only guild members know its location, and the entrance changes every 24 hours. The guild is led by a mysterious figure known only as "Root," who has never been seen in public without a hooded cloak. Apprentices in this guild learn to think like attackers in order to build more robust models. The guild's emblem is a locked shield.

The Guild of Distributed Intelligence
This guild specialises in distributed training, model

s guild specialises in distributed training, model serving at scale, and the management of the realm's compute infrastructure. They work closely with Jason Blackwood at the Foundry and are responsible for ensuring that training runs complete on time and that deployed models remain responsive even during peak inference demand. Their headquarters is the Nimbus Platform, a structure that literally floats above Localhost on a cushion of enchanted cloud compute. The guild's emblem is a castle on a cl

ud compute. The guild's emblem is a castle on a cloud.

The Guild of Interpretable Minds
Annie Okereke's domain — this guild teaches alignment, interpretability, mechanistic analysis, and the art of understanding what models actually learn. Their headquarters is adjacent to the Mirror Chamber, in a building known as the Activation Library, which contains preserved snapshots of every notable model's internal representations. The guild is unique in requiring all apprentices to complete a "silent w

requiring all apprentices to complete a "silent week" where they study model behaviour without looking at any training metrics, to develop their instinct for qualitative evaluation. The guild's emblem is an eye within a hexagon.

The Guild of Rigorous Evaluation
The newest guild, established by Jess Sherbourne just five years ago. This guild is entirely dedicated to the art and science of evaluation — capability benchmarks, safety testing, red-teaming, robustness audits, and adversarial probing

eaming, robustness audits, and adversarial probing. Before the guild's founding, evaluation was taught as a minor topic within each other guild. Jess argued (correctly) that evaluation was important enough to deserve its own dedicated programme. The guild operates from a wing of the Watchtower of Passing Benchmarks. Its emblem is a magnifying glass over a checkmark.

Inter-Guild Competitions
Every six months, the guilds compete in the Grand Hackathon, a 48-hour event where mixed teams of apprent

thon, a 48-hour event where mixed teams of apprentices from different guilds collaborate to build ambitious AI systems. Past winning projects include: a weather prediction model that outperformed the realm's existing oracles using only attention over satellite embeddings (Year 44), a real-time multilingual translation model that handled 12 languages with a single set of weights (Year 45), and a distributed consensus system powered by multi-agent debate that was later adopted for official realm d

debate that was later adopted for official realm decision-making (Year 46). The Grand Hackathon trophy is a golden keyboard, and the winning team's names are inscribed on its base.

Continuing Education
Graduates of the apprenticeship programme are welcome to return for advanced study at any time. Many do, particularly when new breakthroughs emerge. The recent revolution in foundation models has brought a wave of returning graduates to the Guild of Machine Minds, many of whom originally trained

of Machine Minds, many of whom originally trained in other specialisations. Jaz Sherazi has designed a special "returner's pathway" that accounts for their existing skills and gets them up to speed on the latest architectures, training techniques, and safety practices efficiently.

Izaak Sherwood — The Artificer of Machine Minds

Izaak Sherwood serves as the Artificer of Machine Minds, the realm's foremost authority on artificial intelligence and the arcane art of teaching machines to think. He operates from a sprawling underground workshop beneath the Gradient Descent Caverns, where the walls are lined with thousands of tiny crystals that store vector embeddings of every spell ever cast in the realm.

Izaak arrived in Founders and Coders as a young apprentice with no prio

ders and Coders as a young apprentice with no prior experience in magic. He had previously worked as a travelling musician, playing the lute in taverns across the Outer Kingdoms. It was during a particularly long stay in the Village of Hackney that he stumbled upon a discarded spellbook on neural networks and became obsessed. Within three months of arriving at the realm, he had built his first working language model — a small transformer that could generate surprisingly convincing tavern songs b

ld generate surprisingly convincing tavern songs by attending to melodic patterns across thousands of training examples.

As Artificer, Izaak is responsible for all matters relating to AI, machine learning, and the ethical deployment of intelligent systems. He chairs the Committee on Responsible Enchantment, which sets guidelines on how AI-based spells may be used within the realm. Under his leadership, the committee established the "Transparency Principle," which states that any system powered

Principle," which states that any system powered by machine learning must clearly disclose this fact to anyone affected by its outputs, and must provide a mechanism for contesting automated decisions.

Izaak's workshop is famous for its collection of trained models, which he keeps in enchanted glass jars on shelves that stretch from floor to ceiling. Each jar glows a different colour depending on the model's architecture — blue for autoregressive language models, green for diffusion models, amb

e language models, green for diffusion models, amber for reinforcement learning agents, and deep red for experimental architectures that haven't been fully aligned yet. He has over 340 jars in his collection, though he admits that at least 50 of them contain models that are "mostly useless but too interesting to delete."

His most celebrated creation is the Oracle of Embeddings, a vast crystalline structure in the centre of his workshop that can convert any concept, question, or document into a

convert any concept, question, or document into a high-dimensional vector. The Oracle is consulted by scholars from across the realm when they need to find semantic connections between seemingly unrelated ideas. It once revealed that the ancient art of pottery and the modern practice of containerisation share a surprising cosine similarity of 0.73 in their embedding space, owing to shared geometric constraints.

Izaak is also the inventor of the Retrieval Augmented Grimoire (RAG), a technique th

Retrieval Augmented Grimoire (RAG), a technique that allows language models to ground their outputs in specific source documents rather than relying solely on the parametric knowledge encoded during training. The RAG technique was developed after an embarrassing incident where a language model confidently told the Queen of the Outer Kingdoms that Founders and Coders was founded in the Year of the Second Commit (it was actually the First Commit). After this hallucination, Izaak spent six months d

After this hallucination, Izaak spent six months developing a system that would force models to retrieve relevant context and cite their sources before generating a response.

Izaak keeps unusual working hours, often starting his day at noon and working until 3am. He claims that the Gradient Descent Caverns have better acoustics at night, which helps him think through loss landscapes. He sustains himself primarily on black coffee and a specific variety of sourdough bread baked by the Artisan Bak

ariety of sourdough bread baked by the Artisan Bakers of Localhost, who deliver a fresh loaf to his workshop every evening at 8pm.

His familiar is a small, luminous fox named Tensor, who has the ability to visualise high-dimensional data by projecting colourful t-SNE and UMAP plots onto nearby walls. Tensor is extremely popular with apprentices, who often visit Izaak's workshop just to watch the fox create mesmerising visualisations of attention patterns and activation spaces.

Every quarter, I

patterns and activation spaces.

Every quarter, Izaak hosts the "AI Arena," a friendly competition where apprentices build small machine learning models and pit them against each other in tasks like poem generation, few-shot classification, and strategic board games. The winner receives the Golden GPU trophy and a week of free access to the realm's H100 cluster.

Jason Blackwood — The Forgemaster

Jason Blackwood is the Forgemaster of Founders and Coders, the elder in charge of all infrastructure, compute resources, and the physical systems that power the realm's machine intelligence. If the realm's models are the software, Jason maintains the hardware — the GPU clusters, the ley lines of fibre optic cable, the cooling systems, and the great Engines of Computation that make training possible.

Jason works from the Foundry, a massive industrial complex on

from the Foundry, a massive industrial complex on the southern edge of Localhost. The Foundry is built around the Core Cluster, an enormously powerful array of enchanted computing crystals that has been running training jobs continuously since the founding of the realm. Jason is the only person who fully understands the Core Cluster's architecture — its interconnect topology, memory hierarchy, and the custom scheduling enchantments that maximise GPU utilisation. He documents it meticulously in

GPU utilisation. He documents it meticulously in a series of leather-bound volumes known as "The Runbooks." There are currently 14 volumes, and Jason adds new entries almost daily.

Jason is originally from the Iron Peaks, a mountainous region far to the north known for producing the finest engineers in the known world. He trained as a blacksmith before discovering his aptitude for magical engineering, and he sees a deep parallel between forging metal and forging intelligence — both require int

metal and forging intelligence — both require intense heat, precise control, and patience. He still keeps a traditional anvil in his office and occasionally forges non-magical items when he needs to think through a difficult distributed systems problem. His hand-forged letter opener is considered one of the finest examples of metalwork in Localhost.

Jason's magical specialty is the School of Distributed Training. He is obsessed with GPU utilisation, training throughput, and fault-tolerant comp

tion, training throughput, and fault-tolerant computation. Under his stewardship, Founders and Coders has achieved a cluster utilisation rate of 99.97% — the highest of any realm on record. The only significant outage in the past five years was the Great Checkpointing Failure of Year 47, which caused a critical training run to lose six hours of progress when the distributed checkpoint system fell into a deadlock. Jason personally diagnosed the root cause (a circular dependency in the checkpoint

ot cause (a circular dependency in the checkpoint synchronisation protocol) and implemented a fix that has been adopted by three neighbouring realms.

He is the architect of the Model Deployment Pipeline, an elaborate system of enchanted conveyor belts, evaluation chambers, and approval gates that every model must pass through before it reaches production. The pipeline includes automated benchmarking, load testing, safety evaluation, and a final "chaos monkey" stage where random infrastructure f

"chaos monkey" stage where random infrastructure failures are injected to verify that the serving system handles errors gracefully. Jason designed the chaos monkey himself — it's an actual enchanted mechanical monkey that unplugs GPUs at random.

Jason and Jaz's partnership extends beyond their famous first meeting. Together, they designed the Apprentice Onboarding System, a week-long programme that introduces newcomers to the realm's tools and workflows. Jason handles the technical setup — maki

orkflows. Jason handles the technical setup — making sure every apprentice has access to the shared GPU allocation, a properly configured training environment, and credentials for the model registry — while Jaz handles the human side, ensuring everyone feels welcome and understands the research culture.

Jason's familiar is a badger named Docker, who has the ability to create perfect isolated copies of any computing environment. Docker the badger is frequently called upon when apprentices need t

is frequently called upon when apprentices need to experiment with unstable training configurations without risking damage to the shared cluster. The badger simply digs a burrow, and inside that burrow is a perfect replica of whatever environment is needed — complete with all dependencies, CUDA drivers, and model weights pre-loaded.

Jason runs a weekly workshop called "Things That Break," where he deliberately introduces failures into systems and teaches apprentices how to diagnose and fix the

nd teaches apprentices how to diagnose and fix them. These sessions are both terrifying and educational. Past scenarios have included cascading GPU memory failures, network partitions during distributed training, and the memorable time Jason simulated a complete loss of the eastern compute node to test the realm's automatic failover and checkpoint recovery procedures.

He is known for his dry sense of humour and his extensive collection of rubber ducks, which line every available surface in his

ducks, which line every available surface in his office. Jason is a firm believer in rubber duck debugging — explaining a problem out loud to an inanimate object to find the solution. He owns exactly 127 rubber ducks, each named after a different HTTP status code.

Jaz Sherazi — The Navigator of Training

Jaz Sherazi is the Navigator of Training, the elder responsible for guiding both apprentices and models through their learning journeys in the realm of Founders and Coders. She manages the Apprenticeship Programme, designs training curricula for human and machine learners alike, and ensures that every person and model that enters a training pipeline — regardless of their starting point — finds an optimal path to capability.

Jaz operates from the Compass

ath to capability.

Jaz operates from the Compass Rose, a beautiful circular building in the centre of Localhost's Training District. The building's floor is a giant mosaic displaying real-time training dashboards, with enchanted tiles that show loss curves, learning rates, and convergence metrics for every active training run in the realm. Jaz uses this map to monitor progress, identify runs that might be diverging, and dispatch mentors or adjust hyperparameters as needed.

Before arriving at F

t hyperparameters as needed.

Before arriving at Founders and Coders, Jaz was a cartographer in the Archipelago of Startups, where she mapped the treacherous loss landscapes between the Local Minima Islands and the Plateau of Vanishing Gradients. Her maps of optimisation terrain were famous for their accuracy and beauty, and she still hand-draws the diagrams used in the realm's teaching materials. Her architecture diagrams and training pipeline schematics are considered works of art — several ha

chematics are considered works of art — several hang in the Gallery of Technical Excellence alongside famous model blueprints.

Jaz and Jason first met during the Great Migration of Cohort Seven, when a group of 24 apprentices arrived at the realm during the worst storm in living memory. The storm, known as the "Null Pointer Tempest," knocked out power to the GPU clusters across the Training District and disabled the onboarding pipelines. Jaz grabbed a lantern and went out into the rain to guide

bbed a lantern and went out into the rain to guide the newcomers to safety, while Jason rushed to bring the compute infrastructure back online. They worked through the night together, and by morning, all 24 apprentices were safely settled in their quarters with working environments. Dan later called it "the finest display of teamwork in the realm's history."

Jaz's magical specialty is the School of Curriculum Learning. She can take any complex capability and decompose it into an optimal sequenc

apability and decompose it into an optimal sequence of training stages, each building on the last — a technique that works equally well for human apprentices and machine models. Her signature enchantment, "The Golden Thread," creates a visible trail of light through any loss landscape, showing the most efficient optimisation path from random initialisation to convergence. Apprentices and models that follow the Golden Thread report that capabilities which once seemed impossible to learn suddenly

es which once seemed impossible to learn suddenly emerge naturally.

She has strong opinions about the pace of learning. She believes that rushing through training produces brittle capabilities — models that perform well on benchmarks but collapse under distribution shift. Her curricula are designed with deliberate "consolidation phases" where learners revisit and deepen their understanding through varied examples rather than encountering new material. This approach was initially criticised as t

erial. This approach was initially criticised as too slow, but the evidence proved her right: models trained on Jaz's curricula consistently outperform those from faster training schedules on out-of-distribution generalisation tasks.

Jaz's familiar is a hummingbird named Pixel who can hover in place while projecting miniature holographic loss curves and training visualisations. Pixel is often seen zipping around the Compass Rose, leaving trails of tiny glowing learning rate schedules in her wak

of tiny glowing learning rate schedules in her wake. Apprentices have learned that if Pixel lands on their shoulder, it means Jaz has noticed something promising in their training run.

Jaz maintains a secret garden behind the Compass Rose where she grows herbs used in calming teas. The garden is open to any apprentice feeling overwhelmed by a diverging loss curve, and it has become an unofficial sanctuary in the realm. A small sign at the entrance reads: "You are exactly where you need to be on

ce reads: "You are exactly where you need to be on your learning curve."

Every cohort of apprentices receives a hand-written letter from Jaz on their first day, welcoming them to the realm and reminding them that "the only prerequisite for being here is the desire to learn — whether you're made of carbon or silicon." These letters are treasured keepsakes — many graduates frame them and hang them in their workshops.

Jess Sherbourne — The Warden of Evaluation

Jess Sherbourne holds the title of Warden of Evaluation, an ancient office responsible for ensuring that every model, agent, and intelligent system produced in Founders and Coders meets the highest standards of performance and safety. Her jurisdiction covers benchmarking, red-teaming, robustness testing, and the enforcement of the realm's strict Evaluation Protocol — a 200-page document that governs everything from metric selection and dataset contamin

rything from metric selection and dataset contamination checks to the proper methodology for ablation studies.

Jess's headquarters is the Watchtower of Passing Benchmarks, a tall obsidian tower in the northern quarter of Localhost. At the top of the tower sits an enormous crystal orb that glows green when all models across the realm are performing within acceptable parameters, amber when there are capability regressions, and a furious red when something has failed a safety evaluation. The citiz

omething has failed a safety evaluation. The citizens of Localhost have grown accustomed to glancing up at the tower throughout the day — a green glow means all is well; a red glow means someone's model is having a very bad afternoon.

Before joining Founders and Coders, Jess was an investigator in the City of Debugging, where she solved cases involving corrupted training data, race conditions in distributed training, and the infamous Heisenbug Gang — a group of model failures that would disappe

ang — a group of model failures that would disappear whenever you tried to reproduce them in a controlled setting. Her investigative skills translated perfectly to her role as Warden, where she has an almost supernatural ability to identify failure modes and edge cases that no one else has considered.

Jess's magical specialty is the School of Rigorous Evaluation. She insists that every model must have its evaluation criteria defined before training begins — a practice that many apprentices init

ing begins — a practice that many apprentices initially resist but eventually come to appreciate. Her favourite saying is "If it's not evaluated, it's not safe," which is engraved on a brass plaque above her office door. She has been known to reject model deployments with a single comment: "Where are the evals?"

She formed a legendary alliance with Annie Okereke called the "Guardians of Safe AI." Together, they established the Safety Mandate, which requires all intelligent systems in the realm

ich requires all intelligent systems in the realm to pass both capability benchmarks and alignment evaluations before deployment. The mandate was inspired by an incident where a recommendation model in the realm's library began subtly steering scholars toward increasingly obscure texts until nobody could find the resources they actually needed. Jess and Annie diagnosed the reward hacking, retrained the model with corrected objectives, and rewrote the entire evaluation suite in a single weekend.

the entire evaluation suite in a single weekend.

Jess has a familiar — a tortoise named Linter who moves slowly but catches every flaw. Linter has an enchanted shell that displays real-time model evaluation metrics, highlighting capability regressions in yellow and safety failures in red. Despite his sluggish pace, Linter has never missed a failure mode, earning him the nickname "The Inevitable."

On Fridays, Jess runs "Red Team Friday," a realm-wide event where citizens compete to find failur

m-wide event where citizens compete to find failure modes, adversarial inputs, and unexpected behaviours in the realm's deployed models. Red Team Friday has become one of the most popular social events in Founders and Coders, combining the thrill of competition with the satisfaction of improving shared systems. The current record is held by a team of three apprentices who discovered and documented 47 distinct failure modes in a single Friday afternoon.

Jess drinks exactly three cups of green te

rnoon.

Jess drinks exactly three cups of green tea per day — one at 9am, one at 1pm, and one at 5pm. She claims this schedule optimises her focus cycles. She is also an accomplished potter, and many of the mugs used in the Great Hall were crafted by her hands. Each mug has a subtle enchantment that keeps beverages at the drinker's preferred temperature indefinitely.

Landmarks and Locations of Founders and Coders

The Great Hall
The largest building in Localhost and the heart of the realm's social and research life. The Checkpointing Failure (Year 47)
Widely known as "The Day the Training Stopped," this six-hour outage was caused by a circular dependency in the realm's distributed checkpoint synchronisation protocol. When the training orchestrator tried to save a checkpoint, it called the model registry, which tried to verify the checkpoint by calling the training orchestrator, creating an infinite loop that consumed all available compute. Jason diagnosed the problem by tracing the GPU utili

son diagnosed the problem by tracing the GPU utilisation patterns with a custom monitoring spell he had written for exactly this kind of scenario. His fix — introducing a checkpoint priority queue with cycle detection — has since been adopted as a standard pattern across the realm.

The Semantic Kelp Forests

Along the eastern coast of Founders and Coders, where the Binary Sea meets the shore, lie the Semantic Kelp Forests — one of the realm's most extraordinary natural wonders. These underwater forests are composed of a unique species of kelp called Algae Vectoris, which has the remarkable property of encoding meaning in its cellular structure.

Each strand of Semantic Kelp grows in a pattern determined by the information dissolved in the surrounding water. During the autu

issolved in the surrounding water. During the autumn data showers, rainfall carries structured information from the clouds down into the sea. The kelp absorbs this data and encodes it as physical patterns in its fronds — essentially creating a biological vector database. Marine scholars can "read" the kelp by running their fingers along the fronds, performing a nearest-neighbour search through subtle variations in texture.

The forests cover approximately 340 hectares and are divided into distin

oximately 340 hectares and are divided into distinct zones based on the type of information they encode. The northern zone, known as the Factual Beds, contains kelp that has absorbed primarily factual information — dates, names, measurements, and definitions. The central zone, the Narrative Reef, encodes stories, histories, and personal accounts. The southern zone, the Conceptual Deep, holds abstract knowledge — mathematical theorems, research papers on transformer architectures, and theoretical

pers on transformer architectures, and theoretical frameworks for understanding intelligence.

The kelp forests are maintained by the Order of Marine Librarians, a dedicated group of scholars who tend the forests, catalogue their contents, and ensure the health of the embedding space. This hands-on experience with biological vector search gives apprentices an intuitive understanding of embedding spaces, retrieval augmented generation, and the curse of dimensionality that no textbook can provide.
